study_identification.title: Fractionating autism based on neuroanatomical normative modeling

study_characteristics.study_objective: To introduce a novel methodological framework for parsing neuroanatomical subtypes within a large cohort of individuals with autism by combining normative modeling of cortical thickness with spectral clustering, and to validate these subtypes anatomically, clinically, and genetically.

clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Answer: Five neuroanatomical ASD subtypes were identified with distinct cortical thickness deviation patterns (3 decreased, 2 increased CT), showing strong anatomical separability (>90% AUROC), differential clinical associations, and stronger symptom correlations within clusters than across the whole cohort, demonstrating that biological heterogeneity can be quantified and used for clinically relevant stratification.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Answer: The study identified five putative neuroanatomical subtypes of autism using normative modeling of cortical thickness and spectral clustering in 316 individuals with ASD. K=5 yielded highest cluster separability and stability. Three clusters (1, 2, 3; ~57% of cohort) showed widespread decreased CT, while two clusters (4, 5; ~43%) showed increased CT relative to neurotypical patterns. Anatomical separability was high with average pairwise AUROC >90% (P<0.0001, permutation test). Clusters differed in spatial distribution: Cluster 1 (n=60, 43% female, younger age 14.1±5.5) showed decreased CT in anterior premotor cortex; Cluster 2 (n=55, 24% female) had lowest IQ (FIQ 83.4±17.1) and widespread cortical thinning in dorsolateral prefrontal, orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, motor, and temporal cortices, with higher ADHD symptoms (hyperactivity-impulsivity); Cluster 3 (n=65, 26% female, highest IQ FIQ 110.1±13.4) showed reduced CT in temporal gyrus and was the only cluster associated with polygenic risk (ASD and schizophrenia); Clusters 4 (n=55) and 5 (n=81) showed increased CT in posterior parietal and prefrontal cortex respectively. Clinical associations were stronger within clusters than across the cohort: correlations with ADOS-2 RRB, ADI-R, RBS-R, SRS-2, and ADHD symptoms increased in magnitude and additional associations reached significance when analyzed by cluster (e.g., ADI-RRB). Clusters could be discriminated above chance from clinical measures (accuracy=0.32, chance=0.20, AUROC=0.58, P<0.05), with IQ contributing most. Regional analysis showed similar patterns with stronger associations emerging within clusters. Only Cluster 3 showed associations with polygenic scores after FDR correction. Clusters were evenly distributed across sites with no site-related bias. These results demonstrate that aggregating effects across heterogeneous individuals dilutes clinical associations and that biologically-defined stratification reduces heterogeneity in clinical presentation.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Answer: Large amount of missing clinical and behavioral data, leading to reduced sample size for some analyses (243 with complete data vs 316 total, though imputation validated findings); genetics analysis had relatively low statistical power per cluster; data may not be missing at random; no manual edits performed on FreeSurfer reconstructions, which could have improved surface quality in some cases; number of excluded scans not reported; model order (K=5) requires further validation in independent cohorts; no validation of normative model on external neurotypical or ASD cohorts; clustering tested against model orders K=2-10 but not against null distribution of no clusters (due to high dimensionality); findings should be replicated across additional cohorts and validated for ability to predict clinical outcomes or additional biological measures; other LEAP modalities (EEG, eye-tracking, diffusion MRI) not yet assessed; no assessment of within-site or within-family correlation structure in normative modeling.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: Answer: The study demonstrates a methodological framework combining normative modeling with clustering to fractionate heterogeneous clinical cohorts. Key innovation is using normative models to define individual deviations before clustering, which focuses clustering on clinically relevant variation rather than nuisance factors. The approach capitalizes on both dimensional (normative deviations) and categorical (clusters) aspects of neurobiology. Cluster 2 showed overlap with ADHD-related brain alterations, suggesting shared pathophysiological pathways. Association with ADI-social reached significance only across the entire sample (not within subtypes), potentially indicating social deficits as a unifying feature across ASD. Authors are cautious about claiming definitively five subtypes, viewing clustering as a tool to fractionate clinical phenotypes and understand variation. Validation priorities include replication in independent cohorts, prediction of clinical outcomes, and assessment of other LEAP modalities. Up to 70% of ASD individuals have comorbid psychiatric conditions and 30-50% are on stable medications, which were not exclusion criteria to create a realistic cohort. Future utility may lie in stratifying subgroups for testing associations with outcomes (functioning, persistence, non-psychotic psychopathology).

- general_notes.Answer: "This study builds on the authors' previous normative modeling work in ASD (Zabihi et al., 2019, reference 40, Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging). The methodological framework combining normative modeling with spectral clustering represents an important advance in parsing heterogeneity. Six sites: Cambridge (n=40), KCL (n=119), Mannheim (n=26), Nijmegen (n=80), Rome (n=17), Utrecht (n=34). Site-specific clinical characteristics shown in Supplementary Table S1. Acquisition used standard ADNI sequence to minimize site differences. Intellectual disability participants were excluded from NT cohort but included in ASD cohort (up to 316 total ASD participants vs 243 with complete clinical data). Spectral clustering used cosine similarity affinity matrix with 10,000 random initializations, selecting model with minimum inertia. SVM classification used C=0.25, PCA reduction to 10 components, nested cross-validation (10,000 iterations). Imbalanced classes handled via up-sampling (N_test=5, N_training=45 per class). Behavioral correlations computed across whole cohort and within each cluster with FDR correction. Polygenic scores computed using PRSice-2 on 343 ASD (including ID) and 241 NT, adjusted for ancestry PC1-PC4; seven traits assessed (ASD, ADHD, epilepsy, intelligence, neuroticism, schizophrenia, cross-disorder). Genotyping: Illumina Infinium OmniExpress-24v1 (>700K markers); imputation: Michigan Imputation Server with HRC r1.1 2016 European reference panel (17M SNPs). Quality control included sex check, Mendel errors, IBS, SNP call rate >95%, MAF>0.05, LD r²>0.5, HWE p>10⁻⁶. Inbreeding estimated via runs of homozygosity (ROH). Missing data imputation methods compared: Extra Trees, K-Nearest Neighbors, Bayesian Ridge regression outperformed mean/median imputation. Structure coefficients computed to interpret discriminative regions/measures in SVM classifiers. Figure S1 in supplement provides methodological overview flowchart. The study received EU-AIMS (European Autism Interventions) funding and involves large multi-center collaboration (EU-AIMS LEAP Group). Some authors report conflicts of interest with pharmaceutical companies (consultancies, advisory boards, speakers fees) but state work is unrelated."
